title: Ordinary Time
hookLine: ordinary means counted Sundays, the long green growing season

lines: THE BIG DAYS, AND THE FILLER.
cards: Most of life isn't a feast. It's Tuesday. Laundry, emails, the commute, a sandwich at your desk, the same argument about the dishes.
The holy parts of life seem to be the big days: weddings, funerals, Christmas morning. Everything else is filler.

The Catholic calendar has a name for most of the year, and people laugh a little when they first hear it, because it sounds so plain. It's the longest season of all, and it comes around twice. Today: Ordinary Time.

teach.b: Here's the surprise: ordinary doesn't mean plain or boring. It comes from ordinal, as in counted: first, second, third.
The weeks of this season are numbered: the Third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the Twenty-Fifth Sunday, and so on. In Latin the season is called tempus per annum, time through the year.
There are thirty-three or thirty-four of these weeks, in two stretches. The first is short, from the Baptism of the Lord until Ash Wednesday.
The second is long, from after Pentecost all the way to Advent, most of the summer and fall, ending with the feast of Christ the King. The color is green, the color of things growing.
Week by week, the Sunday Gospels walk steadily through Jesus's public life: his parables, his healings, his teaching.
After the great feasts show who Jesus is, Ordinary Time is about following him on regular days.
Paul put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "All whatsoever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father by him."
Catholics have loved saints who made ordinary work holy.

teach.h: GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.
teach.b: Brother Lawrence, a seventeenth-century Carmelite, spent years as the cook in a Paris monastery, and said he felt as close to God among the pots and pans as when kneeling in church.
Thérèse of Lisieux called her way the little way: small things done with great love.
That's the spirit of the green season. Not waiting for a feast. Growing, week by week.

how: In Ordinary Time Catholic priests wear green, the Sundays are numbered, and the Gospel readings walk through Jesus's public ministry week by week.

games.q: you're Brother Lawrence, assigned to the monastery kitchen, though you'd rather be praying in the chapel. what do you do?
o: ask to be moved to the chapel.
rush the cooking to get back to prayer.
make the cooking itself a prayer.
games.why: he said he felt as close to God among the pots and pans as on his knees in church. ordinary work became his prayer.

practice: Think of one job you'll do today that you usually rush through: washing dishes, answering email, folding clothes, driving. Picture doing it slowly, with attention, even with care.
If you pray, offer it to God before you start, the way Brother Lawrence did with his pots and pans; if you don't, just decide to do it well, for someone.

wordCard.voice: Ordinary Time. Not plain time, but counted time: the long green season of numbered Sundays, twice a year. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: time through the year, the Church's official name for Ordinary Time.

carryVoice: Your line: green, growing. Your week: Benediction, spiritual communion, the colors, Advent, Christmas as a season, Epiphany, and Ordinary Time. A full week, done.
